prompt: Each member of the sequence $112002, 11210, 1121, 117, 46, 34, \dots$ is obtained by adding five times the rightmost digit to the number formed by omitting that digit. Determine the billionth ($10^9$th) member of this sequence.

solutions.title: Find the cycle
solutions.body:
Write a member as $x = 10k + y$ with last digit $y$; the next member is $g(x) = k + 5y$.

**The sequence gets trapped below 49.** If $x \le 49$, then $k \le 4$ and $g(x) \le 4 + 5\cdot 9 = 49$; so once a member is at most 49, all later ones are too. The 5th member is 46, so from then on there are only finitely many possible values, and since each member determines the next, the sequence must become periodic.

**Compute.** Continuing from 46:
$$46, 34, 23, 17, 36, 33, 18, 41, 9, 45, 29, 47, 39, 48, 44, 24, 22, 12, 11, 6, 30,$$
$$3, 15, 26, 32, 13, 16, 31, 8, 40, 4, 20, 2, 10, 1, 5, 25, 27, 37, 38, 43, 19,$$
and then $g(19) = 1 + 45 = 46$ again. So from the 5th member on, the sequence repeats with period $42$.

**Locate the billionth member.** Member number $n \ge 5$ equals member number $5 + ((n - 5) \bmod 42)$. Since $10^9 = 42\cdot 23809523 + 34$, we have $10^9 - 5 \equiv 29 \pmod{42}$, so the billionth member equals member number $34$, which is the $30$th entry of the cycle listed above (counting 46 as the 1st): $40$.

**Answer: 40**

solutions.title: Work modulo 49
solutions.body:
With $x = 10k + y$ and $g(x) = k + 5y$:
$$10\,g(x) = 10k + 50y = x + 49y \equiv x \pmod{49}.$$
Since $10 \cdot 5 = 50 \equiv 1$, this says $g(x) \equiv 5x \pmod{49}$: each step multiplies the residue by 5. The first member is $112002 \equiv 37 \pmod{49}$, so the $n$th member $a_n$ satisfies
$$a_n \equiv 37 \cdot 5^{\,n-1} \pmod{49}.$$
Also, from the 5th member on, $1 \le a_n \le 49$ (see the first solution) and $a_n \not\equiv 0$ (as $37\cdot 5^{n-1}$ is not divisible by 7), so $a_n$ is simply the remainder of $37\cdot 5^{n-1}$ modulo 49.

Powers of 5 mod 49: $5^3 = 125 \equiv 27$, $5^6 \equiv 27^2 = 729 \equiv -6$, $5^{12} \equiv 36$, $5^{18} \equiv 36\cdot(-6) = -216 \equiv 29$, $5^{21} \equiv 29 \cdot 27 = 783 \equiv -1$, so $5^{42} \equiv 1$ (this is the period 42). Now $10^9 - 1 \equiv 33 \pmod{42}$, and
$$5^{33} = 5^{21}\cdot 5^{12} \equiv -36 \equiv 13,\qquad a_{10^9} \equiv 37 \cdot 13 = 481 = 9\cdot 49 + 40.$$

**Answer: 40**

prompt: The integer 72 is the first of three consecutive integers 72, 73, and 74, that can each be expressed as the sum of the squares of two positive integers. The integers 72, 288, and 800 are the first three members of an infinite increasing sequence of integers with the above property. Find a function that generates the sequence and give the next three members.

An integer lattice point in the Cartesian plane is a point $(x, y)$ where $x$ and $y$ are both integers. Suppose nine integer lattice points are chosen such that no three of them lie on the same line. Out of all 36 possible line segments between pairs of those nine points, some line segments may contain integer lattice points besides the original nine points. What is the minimum number of line segments that must contain an integer lattice point besides the original nine points? Prove your answer.

solutions.title: Parity classes
solutions.body:
**Lower bound.** Classify lattice points by the parities of their coordinates: (even, even), (even, odd), (odd, even), (odd, odd) — four classes. If two points are in the same class, then their coordinate differences are even, so the midpoint of the segment joining them is a lattice point, and it is not one of the nine points (no three of the nine are collinear). So every pair of chosen points in the same class gives a segment containing an extra lattice point.

If the classes contain $n_1, n_2, n_3, n_4$ of the nine points ($n_1 + n_2 + n_3 + n_4 = 9$), the number of such pairs is $\sum \binom{n_i}{2}$. Moving a point from a larger class to a class smaller by at least 2 never increases this sum, so it is smallest for the most balanced split $3, 2, 2, 2$:
$$\binom32 + \binom22 + \binom22 + \binom22 = 3 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6.$$
(Directly: by pigeonhole some class has at least 3 points; a class with $\ge 4$ points already gives $\binom42 = 6$ pairs; two classes with 3 give $3 + 3 = 6$; otherwise the split is exactly $3, 2, 2, 2$.) So at least 6 segments contain extra lattice points.

**Six is achievable.** Take
$$(0,0),\ (1,6),\ (2,2),\ (2,4),\ (3,7),\ (4,5),\ (5,6),\ (6,5),\ (7,1).$$
A segment between lattice points contains another lattice point exactly when the coordinate differences $\Delta x, \Delta y$ have a common factor $> 1$. Checking all 36 pairs, this happens only for the six same-parity pairs $\{(0,0),(2,2)\}$, $\{(0,0),(2,4)\}$, $\{(2,2),(2,4)\}$, $\{(1,6),(5,6)\}$, $\{(3,7),(7,1)\}$, $\{(4,5),(6,5)\}$ — no two points have differences with a common odd factor. One also checks that no three of the points are collinear.

**Answer: 6**

prompt: Let $f(n)$ be the number of ones that occur in the decimal representations of all the numbers from 1 to $n$. For example, this gives $f(8) = 1$, $f(9) = 1$, $f(10) = 2$, $f(11) = 4$, and $f(12) = 5$. Determine the value of $f(10^{100})$.

solutions.title: Count by digit position
solutions.body:
Consider the numbers $0, 1, \dots, 10^{100} - 1$ written with exactly 100 digits (padding with leading zeros; the padding adds no ones, and including 0 adds none). Every string of 100 digits occurs exactly once. In each of the 100 positions, each digit $0$–$9$ appears equally often, namely $10^{99}$ times. So the number of ones is $100 \cdot 10^{99} = 10^{101}$.

Finally $10^{100}$ itself contributes one more 1:
$$f(10^{100}) = 10^{101} + 1.$$

(Small check: $f(10) = 1\cdot 10^0 + 1 = 2$ and $f(100) = 2\cdot 10 + 1 = 21$ ✓. In general $f(10^n) = n\cdot 10^{n-1} + 1$.)

**Answer: $10^{101} + 1$**

solutions.title: Count numbers by how many ones they have
solutions.body:
Among the 100-digit strings (numbers $0$ to $10^{100} - 1$), those with exactly $i$ ones number $\binom{100}{i}9^{100-i}$, and they contain $i\binom{100}{i}9^{100-i}$ ones. Using $i\binom{n}{i} = n\binom{n-1}{i-1}$ and the binomial theorem:
$$\sum_{i=1}^{100} i\binom{100}{i}9^{100-i} = 100\sum_{j=0}^{99}\binom{99}{j}9^{99-j} = 100(1+9)^{99} = 10^{101}.$$
Adding the 1 in $10^{100}$: $f(10^{100}) = 10^{101} + 1$.

**Answer: $10^{101} + 1$**

prompt: For an isosceles triangle $ABC$ where $AB = AC$, it is possible to construct, using only compass and straightedge, an isosceles triangle $PQR$ where $PQ = PR$ such that triangle $PQR$ is similar to triangle $ABC$, point $P$ is in the interior of line segment $\overline{AC}$, point $Q$ is in the interior of line segment $\overline{AB}$, and point $R$ is in the interior of line segment $\overline{BC}$ (see the figure). Describe one method of performing such a construction. Your method should work on every isosceles triangle $ABC$, except that you may choose an upper limit or lower limit on the size of angle $BAC$.
answer: For $\angle BAC < 90^\circ$: let $P$, $R$ be the midpoints of $AC$, $BC$ and $Q$ the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$. Then $PQ = PR = \frac{AC}2$, $QR = \frac{BC}2$, so $PQR$ is $ABC$ scaled by $\frac12$. (Other constructions work too, e.g. one via the bisector of $\angle B$ for $\angle BAC < 108^\circ$.)

solutions.title: Midpoints and an altitude (for an acute apex angle)
solutions.body:
Assume $\angle BAC < 90^\circ$.

**Construction.**
1. Construct the midpoint $P$ of $AC$ and the midpoint $R$ of $BC$ (with perpendicular bisectors).
2. Drop the perpendicular from $C$ to line $AB$; call its foot $Q$.
3. Draw triangle $PQR$.

**Why it works.**
* $PR$ joins the midpoints of $CA$ and $CB$, so $PR = \frac12 AB = \frac12 AC$.
* Triangle $AQC$ has a right angle at $Q$, and $P$ is the midpoint of its hypotenuse $AC$, so $PQ = \frac12 AC$ (the midpoint of the hypotenuse is the circumcentre).
* Triangle $BQC$ has a right angle at $Q$, and $R$ is the midpoint of its hypotenuse $BC$, so $QR = \frac12 BC$.

So triangle $PQR$ has sides $\frac12 AC, \frac12 AC, \frac12 BC$ with $PQ = PR$: it is similar to $ABC$ (SSS, ratio $\frac12$), with $P$ corresponding to $A$.

**Positions.** $P$ and $R$ are midpoints, so they are interior points of $AC$ and $BC$. The foot $Q$ of the altitude from $C$ lies strictly between $A$ and $B$ exactly when the angles at $A$ and $B$ are both acute. The base angle $B$ is always acute, and $\angle A < 90^\circ$ by assumption. (For $\angle A = 90^\circ$ we would get $Q = A$, and for obtuse $A$, $Q$ falls outside the segment.) ∎

solutions.title: Bisect angle B (works up to 108°)
solutions.body:
Let $\alpha = \angle BAC$ and $\beta = \angle ABC = \angle ACB = 90^\circ - \frac\alpha2$.

**Construction.** Bisect $\angle ABC$; let the bisector meet $AC$ at $P$. At $P$, copy the angle $\frac\alpha2$ (half of the bisected $\angle BAC$) on both sides of ray $PB$; let the two rays meet $AB$ at $Q$ and $BC$ at $R$. Draw $PQR$.

**Why it works.** Triangles $PBQ$ and $PBR$ share side $PB$, and $\angle PBQ = \angle PBR = \frac\beta2$, $\angle BPQ = \angle BPR = \frac\alpha2$; so they are congruent (ASA) and $PQ = PR$. Also $\angle QPR = \alpha = \angle BAC$, so the isosceles triangles $PQR$ and $ABC$ have equal apex angles and hence are similar.

**When Q and R land inside the sides.** In triangle $ABP$, $\angle APB = 180^\circ - \alpha - \frac\beta2 = 135^\circ - \frac{3\alpha}4$. The ray $PQ$ meets the interior of $AB$ iff $\frac\alpha2 < 135^\circ - \frac{3\alpha}{4}$, i.e. $\alpha < 108^\circ$. Similarly $\angle BPC = \alpha + \frac\beta2 > \frac\alpha2$ always, so $R$ is always inside $BC$. Hence this construction works whenever $\angle BAC < 108^\circ$. ∎
